title: The Addition of Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to IP
summary: Specifies adding Explicit Congestion Notification to IP and TCP, including its use of two bits in the IP header. Routers can signal congestion by marking packets instead of dropping them.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of throwing away a letter when the mailroom is crowded, the clerk puts a sticker on it saying slow down.

subtitle: Routers can mark packets to say "slow down" instead of dropping them, using two bits in the IP header and two flags in TCP.

tldr.problem: TCP learns about congestion only when a packet is lost, which builds up queues and hurts delay-sensitive traffic, even though routers with active queue management can detect congestion earlier.
tldr.mechanism: Two bits in the IP header carry an ECN field, so a router can set the Congestion Experienced codepoint instead of dropping an ECN-capable packet. TCP gains a setup negotiation and two header flags, ECN-Echo and CWR, to carry the signal back and forth.
tldr.outcome: The sender reacts to one marked packet as it would to one dropped packet. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the experimental RFC 2481, and later RFCs have updated it.

facts.label: ECN field size
facts.value: 2 bits (bits 6 and 7 of the TOS / Traffic Class octet)

today: RFC 3168 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoleted the experimental RFC 2481 and has since been updated by RFC 4301, RFC 6040, RFC 8311 and RFC 9768.

sections.title: Why Mark Instead of Drop
sections.content:
TCP treats the network as a black box. It increases its window until a packet is lost and treats that loss as the sign of congestion. That works for plain best-effort data, but it makes queues at the bottleneck router build up, and with drop policies such as tail-drop it can cause loss to synchronize across flows. Interactive traffic such as telnet, web browsing and audio and video can be sensitive to losing individual packets, or to the added delay of retransmitting them.

Active queue management (AQM), for example Random Early Detection (RED), detects congestion before the queue overflows by looking at the average queue length. In the absence of ECN, AQM can only signal by dropping a packet. With ECN, the router can set the Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint in the IP header of a packet from an ECN-capable transport instead, so the packet still arrives and no retransmission delay is needed.

The RFC adopts guiding principles: ECN must be incrementally deployable without islands of capable and non-capable systems, must coexist with existing congestion control and dropping, and must not make it easier to turn off TCP congestion control. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 2481, and updates RFC 2474, RFC 2401 and RFC 793.
sections.plainLanguage: When a hallway gets crowded, the old way was to turn some kids away at the door. The new way is to give them a note saying "please walk slower", so nobody gets sent home.

sections.title: The ECN Field in the IP Header
sections.content:
The ECN field is two bits in the IP header, giving four codepoints: 00 Not-ECT, 01 ECT(1), 10 ECT(0) and 11 CE. The data sender sets ECT(0) or ECT(1) to say that both ends of the transport are ECN-capable. Routers treat the two ECT codepoints as equivalent, and senders that only need one SHOULD use ECT(0). Not-ECT means the packet is not using ECN, and a router sets CE to signal congestion.

The field sits in bits 6 and 7 of the IPv4 TOS octet, which corresponds to the IPv6 Traffic Class octet. The first six bits are the Differentiated Services field. Having two ECT codepoints gives a one-bit ECN nonce, which lets a sender check that routers are not erasing CE and that receivers report CE honestly; this document does not define how TCP uses it.

Fragments must not lose congestion information: if any fragment of a packet being reassembled has CE set, the reassembled packet gets CE (unless another fragment is Not-ECT) or the packet is dropped. A pure ACK MUST NOT indicate ECN-capability, and a CE codepoint MUST NOT be reset by a router.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has two tiny boxes for a traffic light. One setting says "I do not understand these signals", another says "I do", and the last says "it got crowded on the way".

sections.title: How Routers Decide to Mark
sections.content:
A router SHOULD only set CE on an ECN-capable packet when it would otherwise have dropped that packet to signal congestion. If the buffer is not yet full and the router is ready to drop a packet to warn of incipient congestion, it first checks for an ECT codepoint, and if present it MAY set CE instead. A router MUST NOT set CE instead of a drop that has other causes, such as an edge node configured to drop a traffic class unconditionally. When the queue is full, the router drops as usual. An already marked CE packet is passed on unchanged.

The response of the end systems to a single CE packet MUST be essentially the same as to a single dropped packet. This keeps treatment fair when some routers drop while others mark. End systems should react at most once per window of data, which is about once per round-trip time.

CE should reflect persistent rather than transient congestion, so routers should not set it from the instantaneous queue size; the RFC points to the average queue size, as in RED. It also recommends that routers drop rather than mark when the average queue size is above an upper threshold, so that marking is only used while the marking rate is reasonably low.
sections.plainLanguage: A teacher who was about to send a noisy kid out of class can instead hand over a warning card. If the room is completely overflowing, she still has to send someone out.

sections.title: TCP Negotiation and Flags
sections.content:
ECN needs transport support. For TCP the RFC adds three things: negotiation at connection setup, an ECN-Echo (ECE) flag so the receiver can tell the sender about a CE packet, and a Congestion Window Reduced (CWR) flag so the sender can tell the receiver it has reacted. They use bits 9 (ECE) and 8 (CWR) of the TCP Reserved field, leaving a 4-bit Reserved field.

The initiating host sends an "ECN-setup SYN" with both ECE and CWR set. The responder sends an "ECN-setup SYN-ACK" with only ECE set. A host MUST NOT set ECT on data packets unless it has sent and received ECN-setup packets and sent no non-ECN-setup SYN or SYN-ACK, and a host MUST NOT set ECT on SYN or SYN-ACK packets. The asymmetry between the two flag patterns protects against a faulty TCP implementation that simply echoes the Reserved field back.

Some firewalls, load balancers and intrusion detection systems drop an ECN-setup SYN or answer with a RST, because they take it for a port-scanning signature. A host that gets a RST, or no reply within the normal SYN retransmission timeout, MAY resend the SYN with CWR and ECE cleared, which may result in a connection without ECN.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the warning cards, both kids must show each other a secret handshake to prove they both know the system. If one grown-up blocks the handshake, they just talk the old way.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Behavior in TCP
sections.content:
With ECN in use, the sender sets an ECT codepoint on new data packets. When the receiver gets a CE packet, it sets ECE in its next ACK, and keeps setting ECE on all ACKs until it receives a packet with CWR. With delayed ACKs, ECE is set if any acknowledged packet was CE. The sender treats an ACK with ECE as it would a congestion loss: it halves the congestion window cwnd and reduces ssthresh, and SHOULD NOT increase the window in response. It reduces at most once per window of data. After a reduction it sets CWR on the first new data packet. If the window is already one MSS, the sender MUST reset the retransmit timer on receiving ECE.

Some packets must not carry ECT. Pure ACKs MUST be sent as Not-ECT, because TCP cannot react to congestion on the ACK path. Retransmitted data packets MUST NOT carry ECT, partly to prevent a denial-of-service attack where a spoofer sends out-of-window data with CE set; receivers SHOULD ignore CE on out-of-window packets. Window probes MUST NOT carry ECT or CWR.
sections.plainLanguage: When the kid at the receiving end gets a warning card, he keeps waving a flag back until the sender shows a sign saying "I slowed down". Only then does he lower the flag.

sections.title: Tunnels and IPsec
sections.content:
In a simple IP tunnel the ECN octet is copied from the inner header to the outer, and the outer header is discarded at the tunnel exit. A CE mark set on the outer header would be lost there, so the tunnel would hide congestion. The RFC gives two options. The limited-functionality option sets Not-ECT in the outer header and leaves the inner header unchanged, so congestion inside the tunnel can only be shown by drops. The full-functionality option copies Not-ECT or ECT from the inner header to the outer one (CE inside becomes ECT(0) outside), and at the exit sets CE in the inner header if the outer header has CE.

All IP tunnels MUST implement the limited-functionality option and SHOULD support the full-functionality option. For IPsec tunnel mode the same applies. The RFC adds an optional ECN Tunnel field to the Security Association Database and an optional Security Association attribute, with value 10 allocated, to negotiate ECN use. Because IPsec's cryptographic checks do not cover the ECN field, IPsec cannot defend against someone altering it, and running in limited-functionality mode is the way to remove a covert channel.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter travels inside a second envelope, a sticker on the outer envelope would be thrown away with it. So the rules say how to copy the sticker to the inner letter, or to skip the outer sticker entirely.

sections.title: Misbehaving Nodes and Security
sections.content:
The RFC argues that ECN adds little to the existing problem of non-compliant end nodes, and that dropping is not an effective deterrent anyway. It also recommends that a "penalty box" that finds a flow ignoring congestion control first switch from marking to dropping packets for that flow.

A broken or malicious router can alter the ECN field. Falsely reporting congestion, or disabling ECN-capability on a packet, is no worse than dropping it. Erasing a CE mark or falsely claiming ECN-capability can do more harm, because it can defeat congestion control for that flow. On IPv6 there is no header checksum, so bit errors in the ECN field are not caught that way. The RFC's Security Considerations section simply points to its Sections 7, 8, 18 and 19, which analyze these cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky helper could remove the warning sticker or add a fake one. Adding a fake one is like throwing the letter away, which is annoying but not worse. Removing a real one is the dangerous trick.
